nodes.name: Acidic Interface Model Construction
nodes.procedure: Periodic slab model including four layers of Pt(111) in 3×3 supercells, of which the bottom three layers were fixed to the bulk atomic positions. Monolayer of water in hexagonal arrangement representing acidic conditions with H₃O⁺ as proton source, assuming sufficient solvation of the proton by surrounding waters.

nodes.name: Alkaline Interface Model Construction
nodes.procedure: Bilayer of water including a Na⁺ cation, representing NaOH alkaline solutions, constructed on Pt(111) surface. Distance between Na⁺ ion and Pt(111) surface maintained at more than 4.2 Å to prevent specific adsorption while allowing partial desolvation.

nodes.description: Computational DFT and microkinetic modeling of HER/HOR pH effects
nodes.source_text: Table 1. Activation Energies and Tafel Slopes of HER over Pt(111) from Different Proton Sources H3O+/Pt(111): GaVolmer (eV) 0.04, GaHeyrovsky (eV) 0.20, β(|el|) 0.74, Tafel slope (meV/dec) 80; H2O/Na/Pt(111): GaVolmer (eV) 0.42, GaHeyrovsky (eV) 1.20, β(|el|) 0.59, Tafel slope (meV/dec) 100. Our Tafel barrier is 0.72 eV, and the chemical water dissociation has a barrier of 1.02 eV.

nodes.characterization_summary: Hydrogen binding energy E_ads(H/Pt) on Pt(111) calculated as -0.20 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: E_ads(H / Pt) is our computed hydrogen binding energy on Pt(111) and has a value of -0.20 eV.

nodes.characterization_summary: OH adsorption energy on Pt(533) is field-dependent; more negative fields weaken OH adsorption.
nodes.evidence_snippet: We find that the OH adsorption energy is indeed field dependent, following the anticipated relation of more negative field weakening the OH adsorption. The computed relation is shown in Figure 2.

nodes.characterization_summary: HER activation barriers over Pt(111): H3O+ Volmer 0.04 eV, Heyrovsky 0.20 eV (work function 4.4 eV); H2O/Na+ Volmer 0.42 eV, Heyrovsky 1.20 eV (work function 3.6 eV). Tafel barrier 0.72 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The computed proton transfer barriers from H3O+ and H2O are reported at work functions of 4.4 and 3.6 eV, respectively, are summarized in Table 1.
